summary: Proposes experimental improvements for IP multicast in a Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain: a multicast tree mobility anchor as the anchor point for multicast traffic, and a direct routing option where the access gateway gets content from the local network. The goals are less duplicated traffic and support for varied deployments.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7028 adds multicast support to Proxy Mobile IPv6. It offers two ways to get multicast content to a mobile node: pull it down a tunnel from a dedicated multicast anchor, or take it straight from a multicast router on the local network. A new option in the mobility signalling lets the anchor tell the gateway which way to go for each group.

questions: what is a multicast tree mobility anchor
how does multicast work in proxy mobile ipv6
subtitle: Two ways to deliver multicast traffic to a mobile node in a Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain, and the option that chooses between them.

tldr.problem: In a Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain the same multicast traffic can arrive at a mobile access gateway more than once, because the gateway may hold several tunnels to different anchors. That is the tunnel convergence problem.
tldr.mechanism: The memo proposes two complementary schemes: a multicast tree mobility anchor that sits at the topological anchor point for multicast traffic, and direct routing, where the gateway takes its multicast traffic from a local multicast router.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document. The memo says the status may be reconsidered once implementation feedback and deployment experience are available.

today: RFC 7028 is an Experimental document from September 2013, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo says the status of the proposal may be reconsidered in the future, once implementation feedback and deployment experience have been gathered, reporting on the performance of the two schemes and on operational feedback about scheme selection.

sections.title: Introduction and Terminology
sections.content:
Proxy Mobile IPv6 is a network-based approach to solving the IP mobility problem. In a PMIPv6 domain the Mobile Access Gateway behaves as a proxy mobility agent in the network and performs the mobility management on behalf of the Mobile Node, and the Local Mobility Anchor is the home agent for the node and the topological anchor point. PMIPv6 was originally designed for unicast traffic, although a PMIPv6 domain may handle data from both unicast and multicast sources.

IGMPv3 is used by IPv4 hosts to report their IP multicast group memberships to neighbouring multicast routers, and Multicast Listener Discovery Version 2 is used in a similar way by IPv6 routers. The IGMP and MLD proxy specification allows an intermediate node to appear as a multicast router to downstream hosts and as a host to upstream multicast routers. Those protocols were not originally designed to address the IP mobility of multicast listeners, which were assumed to sit on fixed networks.

A base solution supporting both IPv4 and IPv6 multicast listener mobility in a PMIPv6 domain is specified elsewhere, describing deployment options without modifying the mobility and multicast protocol standards. PMIPv6 allows a mobile access gateway to establish multiple PMIPv6 tunnels with different local mobility anchors, for example up to one per mobile node. In the presence of multicast traffic, multiple instances of the same traffic can converge to the same gateway, which may lead to redundant traffic at a gateway. That is the tunnel convergence problem, and it is what this memo addresses.

The memo proposes an experimental solution consisting of two complementary enhancements, a multicast anchor and direct routing. The first uses a Multicast Tree Mobility Anchor as the topological anchor point for remotely delivering multicast traffic, and the second uses direct routing, taking advantage of local multicast source availability so that a gateway can connect directly to a multicast router for simple access to local content. Neither scheme has any impact on the mobile node's support for IPv4 and IPv6 multicast listener mobility, nor on the wider Internet, since they only affect the PMIPv6 domains where they are deployed.

The terminology distinguishes a PMIPv6 unicast domain, the network covered by one Local Mobility Anchor for unicast service, from a PMIPv6 multicast domain, the network covered by one Multicast Tree Mobility Anchor for multicast service, in such a way that a mobile node using that service is not aware of mobility as it moves between gateways. A PMIPv6 domain can have several of each. A Hybrid-LMA is an entity dedicated to both unicast and multicast services, able to work as both anchors at once.
sections.plainLanguage: Proxy Mobile IPv6 lets the network move a mobile node's session around instead of the node itself. The trouble is that a gateway can end up with several tunnels carrying the same multicast stream, so the same content arrives more than once. This memo offers two ways to avoid that.

sections.title: The Two Delivery Modes
sections.content:
The memo describes two complementary operational modes for delivering multicast traffic in a PMIPv6 domain, and the choice between them can be made in different ways depending on the operator's preferences and the deployment characteristics. The mode can be configured manually at the mobile access gateway, following the operator's configuration of the multicast distribution in the domain. Another option is the use of dynamic policies conveyed in the Proxy Binding Update and Proxy Binding Acknowledgement signalling, using the Dynamic IP Multicast Selector option.

In the multicast tree mobility anchor mode, the anchor serves as the mobility anchor for multicast traffic. It is either a designated multicast router or an MLD proxy, and it is typically used to get access to remote multicast content. It connects to the mobile access gateway and can reuse native PMIPv6 features such as tunnel establishment and security, and heartbeat. Unicast traffic goes normally to the local mobility anchors, and a gateway connecting to the anchor acts as an MLD proxy. The anchor can be considered a form of upstream multicast router with tunnel interfaces that allow subscription via the anchor for the mobile nodes. A gateway may connect to both a unicast anchor and a multicast anchor, so a given mobile node may simultaneously receive both unicast and multicast traffic.

In the direct routing mode, the native multicast infrastructure is used, and the gateway connects directly to a multicast router as its next hop within the PMIPv6 domain. A gateway acts as an MLD proxy here too. The main purpose of direct routing is to provide optimal connectivity for local content, and as a consequence it replaces the anchor in the channel management and data delivery of locally available content. Unicast traffic goes as normal to the local mobility anchors.

Each gateway has a direct connection with a multicast router, that is, one that does not use the PMIPv6 tunnel interface. Depending on the multicast support on the visited network, different schemas can provide that connection, such as being on the same shared link, or tunnelling with Generic Routing Encapsulation or Automatic Multicast Tunneling. To facilitate the multicast signalling and forwarding, an MLD proxy function should be implemented in the gateway, and there should be direct connectivity between the gateway and the local multicast router or an additional MLD proxy.
sections.plainLanguage: Mode one pulls the content down a tunnel from a dedicated multicast anchor, which suits content held somewhere else. Mode two takes the content from a multicast router on the local network, which suits content held locally. The gateway behaves as a listener-discovery proxy in both cases, so the mobile node sees nothing different.

sections.title: Mobile Access Gateway Operation
sections.content:
The gateway must maintain a Binding Update List, as specified for PMIPv6, to handle the relationship between the serving entities, such as the multicast anchor and the local mobility anchor, and the mobile nodes, for both unicast and multicast traffic.

In the anchor mode, all gateways connected to the anchor must support the MLD proxy function. Each tunnel interface between a gateway and the anchor defines an MLD proxy domain, with the mobile nodes on the downstream interface of the proxy at the gateway and the anchor on the upstream interface. When a mobile node attaches to a gateway, the gateway first establishes the PMIPv6 tunnel with the local mobility anchor for unicast traffic, triggered by the Router Solicitation from the node, and unicast traffic then flows between the node and that anchor. For multicast traffic, a multicast tunnel may have been pre-configured between the gateway and the multicast anchor, or may be established dynamically when the first mobile node appears at the gateway.

The mobile node sends an MLD Report message, when its upper-layer applications require it, in response to an MLD Query from the gateway, which is generated on handover. The gateway, acting as an MLD proxy, then sends an Aggregated MLD Report to the multicast anchor, if this is a new multicast group the gateway had not previously subscribed to. Multicast traffic then flows from the anchor towards the node. The anchor acts as an MLD Querier, so it periodically queries each gateway about the subscriptions it maintains.

When a node with an ongoing subscription moves from one gateway to another, the new gateway in its role of MLD proxy sends an MLD Query to the newly observed node on its downlink. If the resulting Report asks for a new group from the new gateway's point of view, an Aggregated MLD Report is sent to the anchor through a multicast tunnel between the new gateway and the anchor. When the node detaches, the old gateway may keep the multicast tunnel if other nodes are still using it, and even when there are no nodes currently on the tunnel it may keep it temporarily for potential future use.

In the direct routing mode, the MLD proxy instance is configured to obtain the multicast traffic locally. The gateway establishes the PMIPv6 tunnel with the local mobility anchor for unicast traffic as before, and the upstream interface of the MLD proxy instance is configured to point at a multicast router inside the PMIPv6 domain, or at an additional MLD proxy node, for all the multicast channels, which must therefore be local. On detecting a node attachment from an incoming interface, the gateway adds that interface to the MLD proxy instance with an upstream link to a multicast router and sends an MLD Query towards the node. The node replies with an MLD Report when its applications require it, and the gateway checks the proxy instance associated with the downstream interface, aggregates the reports and forwards them to the upstream link associated with the multicast router, if this is a new group the gateway had not previously subscribed to. Multicast traffic then flows from the local multicast router towards the node.

On handover in the direct routing mode, the new gateway detects the newly arrived node and performs the binding update procedure with the local mobility anchor, while an MLD proxy instance sends an MLD Query to the node. The node replies with an MLD Report including the group information, and the new gateway sends an aggregated MLD Report to the upstream link associated with the multicast router. The upstream interface may be chosen according to dynamic policies conveyed in the Dynamic IP Multicast Selector option or according to manually configured policies, whereas in the base solution the interface is determined for each node from the Binding Update List. When the new gateway receives the multicast packets from the multicast router it forwards them without tunnel encapsulation.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway listens for the mobile node's group subscriptions and passes them upstream, aggregated, so the network carries one copy of the subscription rather than one per node. When the node moves, the new gateway repeats that, and the old one may keep its tunnel for a while in case another node is still there.

sections.title: The Dynamic IP Multicast Selector Option
sections.content:
The memo defines a new TLV-encoded mobility option, the Dynamic IP Multicast Selector option, for use in the Proxy Binding Acknowledgement message exchanged between an anchor and a gateway, to convey dynamic policies on subscription via the anchor or by direct routing. The option is used to exchange the IP addresses of both the group subscribed to by the mobile node and the source or sources delivering it, as well as the applicable filter mode. This information uses the Multicast Address Record format defined for MLD. There can be multiple such options in one message, up to one for each active subscription maintained by the mobile node.

The option has a Type field, whose value is 54, and a Length field giving the length of the option in octets, excluding the type and length fields. The Protocol field identifies the multicast membership protocol in use and the corresponding format of the following Multicast Address Record; it maps the type codification used in the original MLD Report messages, so the value must be 143 for MLDv2 and 131 for MLDv1. The Mode flag, called the M-bit, indicates the subscription mode: when set to 1 the multicast traffic associated with the groups in the option should be routed locally, which is direct routing, and when set to 0 it should be routed to the home network via the anchor. The gateway may also use static pre-established policies instead of following the indications from the anchor, and all other IP traffic associated with the node is managed according to a default policy configured in the PMIPv6 multicast domain.

The Reserved field is unused for now, and must be initialized to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver. The number of Multicast Address Records field is a 16-bit unsigned integer giving the number of records present, and each record carries the multicast subscription information for a single multicast address, as defined for MLDv2 or, for MLDv1, as defined in the earlier MLD specification.
sections.plainLanguage: This option travels in the reply the anchor sends when the gateway registers a node. It lists the groups the node wants, and for each one says whether the content should be fetched from the home network or from somewhere local.

sections.title: The Multicast Tree Mobility Anchor
sections.content:
The anchor provides connectivity to the multicast infrastructure outside the PMIPv6 domain. It can act as an additional MLD proxy, in the case where all the connected gateways also act as MLD proxies, reporting to a further node an aggregated view of the subscriptions in a PMIPv6 multicast domain, or it can act as a designated multicast router for all the gateways in the domain. The anchor then requests the multicast content on behalf of the gateways and the nodes behind them, and creates and maintains the corresponding multicast forwarding states for each tunnel interface towards the gateways. Whatever role it plays, when the gateways act as MLD proxies the anchor becomes the MLD querier of the MLD proxy instance located in each gateway.

The anchor does not directly interact with the mobile nodes attached to the gateways. It only manages the multicast groups subscribed per gateway on behalf of the nodes attached to it. The relevant information to store is the tunnel interface identifier of the bidirectional tunnel for multicast between the anchor and every gateway, the IP addresses of the multicast group delivered per tunnel to each gateway, and the IP addresses of the sources injecting the multicast traffic per tunnel into the multicast domain defined by the anchor.

The mobile node itself is not affected by the existence of the anchor or by the use of direct routing, and acts as specified in the PMIPv6 and base-solution documents. The memo considers that every mobile node requesting multicast-only services is previously registered in a PMIPv6 unicast domain to get a unicast IP address, for purposes such as remote management, billing and multicast configuration, and that the node's policy profile information must be updated so that it can store the IPv6 addresses of both the local mobility anchor and the multicast tree mobility anchor.
sections.plainLanguage: The anchor sits at the top of the multicast tree and keeps a note of which groups each gateway's tunnel is carrying. The mobile node needs no changes at all: it registers for unicast as before and then asks for its multicast groups as usual.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo describes two complementary operational modes and different approaches to deciding which one is selected: the use of pre-configured policies at the mobile access gateway, or the use of dynamic policies. The second approach could introduce a potential security issue if the protocol signalling is not properly secured. The use of the Dynamic IP Multicast Selector option requires message integrity protection and source authentication, so the IPsec security mechanism recommended by Proxy Mobile IPv6 must be used to secure the option conveyed in the Proxy Binding Acknowledgement.

The memo says the document introduces no additional security threats beyond the current security considerations of PMIPv6, MLD, IGMP and IGMP/MLD proxying. For IPv4 support, all the described network elements, the gateway, the anchor and the multicast router, must support IGMP, and the multicast router must also be dual-stack enabled. The Protocol field of the option maps the type codification used in the original IGMP Report messages: it must be 0x12 for IGMPv1, 0x16 for IGMPv2 and 0x22 for IGMPv3. The Multicast Address Record takes different formats depending on the IGMP version used by the mobile node.
sections.plainLanguage: The only new risk is that the anchor tells the gateway which way to fetch each group, so that advice has to be protected. The memo requires the same IPsec protection that Proxy Mobile IPv6 already uses, and says no new threats come with the scheme itself.
